With the HEDS operation, the CRC water reheat provides a direct offset to the VAV reheat load required, and the total thermal load provided by the chiller is significantly reduced. Referring to Fig. 4, the Space load profiles look rather similar for the HEDS and corresponding baseline modes, except for the VAV HEDS mode. The reason for this difference in the building load profile during the VAV HEDS mode is that the HEDS HVAC system optimization package uses the Thermal Flywheel code and allows the average zone temperature to be set back to 67 °F, whereas it is held much more constant at approximately 70 °F in the other modes, as was seen in Fig. 3. Since the evaluations were performed during normal operations at the museum with variations in building occupancy as well as daily weather variations, there are differences in the loads that are not accounted for in this data. The results in Figure 4 clearly show the benefits of the HEDS operation during the field evaluation at the Timken Museum. With the recovery coil enabled in both the VAV HEDS and CAV HEDS modes, the reheat coil loads at the VAV boxes decreased significantly compared to the corresponding baseline modes. It is seen that the CRC reheat, which is shown as a negative value in Figure 4, provides a very direct offset to the total cooling load requirement (HEDS water side load) from the baseline configurations. For the periods evaluated, the CRC reheat coil recovered, on average, approximately 25% of the cooling coil load in the VAV HEDS mode and 30% in the CAV HEDS mode (total cooling coil load includes the CRC reheat and the net AHU load). Figure 5 shows a comparison of the outside air, return air, and mixed air temperatures during all measurement periods. The temperature of the mixed air is quite similar to that of the return air, indicating that the outdoor air (ventilation) load is very minor.
